A one-to-one textual notation for a specific processor's machine code. One line, one
instruction, one opcode; the mnemonics and the [[Motorola 68000]]'s bit patterns are the same
thing written two ways. That is what separates it from a compiled language, where one line of
C becomes however many instructions the compiler felt like.

Which also means assembly is **not portable**. 68000 assembly runs on a 68000 and nowhere
else, because you are writing that chip's [[Computer Architecture|instruction set]] directly.

## The pieces of a line

```
label:  move.l  #5,d0        ; comment
  ^       ^      ^   ^
label   opcode  src dest
```

Four columns: an optional label (a name for this address), the mnemonic with its size suffix
`.b` / `.w` / `.l`, the operands, and a comment. Source first, destination second, which is
the opposite of Intel syntax if you meet it later.

## The toolchain

Source goes through an **assembler** to an object file, then a **linker** joins object files
and resolves cross-references into an executable. The split is why [[Assembly Errors]] has an
assembly-time category (syntax, this file) and a link-time one (unresolved references, all
files together): the assembler cannot know whether a label defined elsewhere exists.

## Why learn it

Not to write programs in it. To have somewhere concrete to stand: [[Pointer]]s stop being
mysterious once you have written `(a0)`, a [[Data type]] stops being magic once you have
chosen `.b` yourself, and the errors in [[C]] make sense once you have seen the machine
produce them. It also stays useful in the places where nothing else fits: device drivers,
[[ISRs]], boot code, and anywhere the exact cycle count matters.

[[Assembly]] is the whole reason [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] can talk about hardware without
hand-waving.
